title: 方波的频谱与对称性
statement: 电压源 u_s 是幅值 U_m = 10 V、频率 f = 50 Hz 的对称方波：0 < t < T/2 时 u_s = +10 V，T/2 < t < T 时 u_s = −10 V（T = 20 ms）。它接在电阻 R = 100 Ω 上。
这个方波的傅里叶级数为 u_s = \frac{4U_m}{π}(sin ωt + \frac{1}{3}sin 3ωt + \frac{1}{5}sin 5ωt + …)。计算时取到 99 次谐波。
回答关于它的频谱的几个问题（振幅指各次谐波的幅值）。

questions.ask: 这个方波含有哪些分量？
choices: 只有奇次谐波，没有直流分量
奇次、偶次谐波都有，没有直流分量
直流分量、基波和 3 次谐波
choiceExplain: 偶次谐波为零是因为波形**半波对称**：f(t + T/2) = −f(t)。
一个周期内正负面积相等，平均值（直流分量）不可能不为零；偶次谐波也要先检查波形是否半波对称。
方波的频谱是无穷的：所有奇次谐波都有，只是振幅按 1/k 减小。
questions.explain: u_s 在一个周期内正负面积相等，所以 a_0 = 0；又满足 f(t + T/2) = −f(t)（半波对称，也叫奇谐波函数），所以只含奇次谐波。

questions.ask: 以图中的计时起点，傅里叶级数里出现的是哪种项？
choices: 只有正弦项 sin kωt（换成 cos 参考时初相为 −90°）
choiceExplain: 余弦项对应偶函数 f(−t) = f(t)；这里 f(−t) = −f(t)，是奇函数。
正弦、余弦项都有是没有对称性的一般波形；这个方波满足 f(−t) = −f(t)，要按奇函数的性质去掉一类系数。
questions.explain: f(−t) = −f(t)：u_s 是奇函数，所有 a_k = 0，只有 b_k sin kωt。改变计时起点（例如让 t = 0 落在正半周中间）会把它变成偶函数，频谱的振幅不变、只有初相改变。
U_1m = 4U_m/π = 40/π ≈ 12.73 V——比方波本身的幅值 10 V 还大。
U_3m = U_1m/3 = 40/(3π) ≈ 4.244 V：方波第 k 次谐波的振幅是 4U_m/(kπ)。

questions.ask: u 的有效值 U = ?（可以用方波的定义直接算，不必把各次谐波加起来）
questions.explain: u² 恒等于 100 V²，所以 U = √(\frac{1}{T}∫_{0}^{T} u² dt) = 10 V。用谐波算：U² = Σ U_km²/2，取到 99 次时为 9.98 V，与 10 V 只差 0.2%。

hints: 先看两种对称性：f(−t) 与 f(t) 的关系决定只有正弦项还是只有余弦项；f(t + T/2) 与 f(t) 的关系决定偶次谐波是否为零。
直流分量就是一个周期内的平均值；k 次谐波的振幅可以直接从题目给出的级数读出：前面的系数 4U_m/π 乘以 1/k。
有效值按定义 U² = \frac{1}{T}∫_{0}^{T} u² dt 来算，方波的 u² 是常数。
solution: **1. 对称性。** u_s(−t) = −u_s(t)，是**奇函数**，所以余弦系数 a_k = 0，级数里只有 sin kωt。又 u_s(t + T/2) = −u_s(t)，**半波对称**，所以 a_0 = 0 且所有偶次谐波为零。结论：只有奇次谐波的正弦项。
**2. 振幅。** 由级数，k 次（k 为奇数）谐波振幅 U_km = 4U_m/(kπ)：
用余弦参考写成 u_s = Σ U_km cos(kωt − 90°)，每一项的初相都是 −90°。
**3. 有效值。** 方波的 u² ≡ U_m²，U = U_m = **10 V**。
**检查：** 用谐波计算 U² = Σ U_km²/2 = \frac{8U_m²}{π²}(1 + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{25} + …) = \frac{8U_m²}{π²}·\frac{π²}{8} = U_m²，两种方法一致。取到 99 次时得 9.98 V，说明有限项的级数已经足够精确。

en.title: Spectrum and symmetry of a square wave
statement: The source u_s is a symmetric square wave of amplitude U_m = 10 V and frequency f = 50 Hz: u_s = +10 V for 0 < t < T/2 and u_s = −10 V for T/2 < t < T (T = 20 ms). It is connected to a resistor R = 100 Ω.
Its Fourier series is u_s = \frac{4U_m}{π}(sin ωt + \frac{1}{3}sin 3ωt + \frac{1}{5}sin 5ωt + …). The calculation keeps harmonics up to the 99th.
Answer the questions about its spectrum (amplitude = peak value of each harmonic).
hints: Look at two symmetries first: how f(−t) relates to f(t) decides between sine-only and cosine-only terms; how f(t + T/2) relates to f(t) decides whether the even harmonics vanish.
The DC component is the average over one period; the amplitude of harmonic k can be read straight from the given series: the factor 4U_m/π times 1/k.
Compute the rms value from its definition U² = \frac{1}{T}∫_{0}^{T} u² dt; for a square wave u² is constant.
solution: **1. Symmetry.** u_s(−t) = −u_s(t): an **odd function**, so every cosine coefficient a_k = 0 and only sin kωt appears. Also u_s(t + T/2) = −u_s(t): **half-wave symmetry**, so a_0 = 0 and all even harmonics vanish. Result: odd-harmonic sine terms only.
**2. Amplitudes.** From the series, harmonic k (k odd) has amplitude U_km = 4U_m/(kπ):
- U_3m = 40/(3π) = **4.244 V** (U_5m = 2.546 V, … the amplitudes fall as 1/k).
In the cosine reference u_s = Σ U_km cos(kωt − 90°): every term has initial phase −90°.
**3. rms value.** For a square wave u² ≡ U_m², so U = U_m = **10 V**.

**Check:** from the harmonics, U² = Σ U_km²/2 = \frac{8U_m²}{π²}(1 + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{25} + …) = \frac{8U_m²}{π²}·\frac{π²}{8} = U_m²; the two methods agree. With 99 harmonics the sum gives 9.98 V: the truncated series is already accurate.

questions.ask: Which components does this square wave contain?
choices: Odd harmonics only, no DC component
Both odd and even harmonics, no DC component
A DC component and even harmonics
A DC component, the fundamental and the 3rd harmonic
choiceExplain: The even harmonics vanish because the wave has **half-wave symmetry**: f(t + T/2) = −f(t).
The positive and negative areas over a period are equal, so there can be no non-zero average (DC component); for even harmonics, check first whether the wave is half-wave symmetric.
A square wave has an infinite spectrum: every odd harmonic is present, with amplitudes falling as 1/k.
questions.explain: u_s has equal positive and negative areas over a period, so a_0 = 0; it also satisfies f(t + T/2) = −f(t) (half-wave symmetry), so it contains odd harmonics only.

questions.ask: With the time origin of the figure, which terms appear in the Fourier series?
choices: Sine terms sin kωt only (initial phase −90° in the cosine reference)
choiceExplain: Cosine terms belong to even functions f(−t) = f(t); here f(−t) = −f(t), an odd function.
Both kinds of term appear only for a waveform without symmetry; this square wave satisfies f(−t) = −f(t), and an odd function loses one set of coefficients.
questions.explain: f(−t) = −f(t): u_s is odd, all a_k = 0, only b_k sin kωt remain. Moving the time origin (e.g. to the middle of the positive half) makes it even: the amplitudes stay the same, only the initial phases change.
U_1m = 4U_m/π = 40/π ≈ 12.73 V — larger than the 10 V of the square wave itself.
U_3m = U_1m/3 = 40/(3π) ≈ 4.244 V: the k-th harmonic of a square wave has amplitude 4U_m/(kπ).

questions.ask: rms value of u, U = ? (use the definition of the square wave directly instead of adding up harmonics)
questions.explain: u² is constantly 100 V², so U = √(\frac{1}{T}∫_{0}^{T} u² dt) = 10 V. From the harmonics, U² = Σ U_km²/2, which gives 9.98 V with 99 harmonics — 0.2 % below 10 V.
